summary: Defines a data model and JSON representation for calendar data, meant to be unambiguous, extensible, and simple to process. It aims to be an alternative to, and over time a successor to, the widely used iCalendar format.

eli5.summary: A modern way to write down events and meetings in JSON, so calendar programs can share them more easily than with the older format.

questions: how does jscalendar handle recurring events
subtitle: A JSON data model for events, tasks and groups, designed to be simpler and less ambiguous than iCalendar.

tldr.problem: iCalendar has ambiguities and pitfalls that cannot be fixed without breaking compatibility, and jCal, its direct JSON mapping, inherits them. Many services came up with incompatible proprietary JSON formats instead.
tldr.mechanism: JSCalendar defines its own data model for Event, Task and Group objects as I-JSON, built from simple key-value properties, with patches for recurring-event exceptions and translations.
tldr.outcome: It is meant to be an alternative to iCalendar and, over time, its successor. It is a Proposed Standard, registers the application/jscalendar+json media type and creates three IANA registries.

today: RFC 8984 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It describes itself as an alternative to, and over time a successor of, iCalendar.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Goals
sections.content:
RFC 8984 defines a data model for calendar events, tasks and groups of them, plus a JSON representation. The format aims to be unambiguous, extendable and simple to process.

The key design considerations are:

  • Attributes are simple key-value pairs, so simple events are simple and complex events can still be modeled accurately.
  • Wherever possible there is only one way to express a given meaning.
  • The model avoids ambiguities that cause interoperability problems.
  • It stays generally compatible with iCalendar, adding attributes where iCalendar lacks expressivity and dropping seldom-used, obsolete or redundant ones, so translation of common files loses little.
  • Extensions should not require updates to this document.

The representation uses I-JSON (RFC 7493), a strict subset of JSON (RFC 8259). The authors call JSON a pragmatic choice: it is widely used, and mature parsers remove a whole class of parser-related interoperability problems that iCalendar has often suffered from.
sections.eli5: The goal is one clear way to write down a meeting, so every calendar app understands it the same way.

sections.title: Why Not iCalendar or jCal?
sections.content:
RFC 5545 iCalendar is widely deployed but has pitfalls that cannot be overcome without backward-incompatible changes. The RFC lists these sources of errors:

  • Different formats for local times, UTC and dates.
  • Custom time zone definitions required inside a single calendar component.
  • Recurrence rules whose ambiguous definition has led to differing interpretations, even among experienced developers.
  • Misuse of CRLF-terminated strings, line continuations, and subtle differences among parsers.

jCal (RFC 7265) maps iCalendar directly to JSON, so it inherits all the same pitfalls and uses a complicated JSON structure. According to the RFC, most implementations either kept using iCalendar or built proprietary JSON formats that are incompatible with each other. Some of these store event start times in UTC, which becomes incorrect if the time zone's rules later change. JSCalendar is a standard alternative free of those known problems.
sections.eli5: The old format is like a recipe full of unclear steps. Cooks read it differently and get different dinners. The new one is written so everyone cooks the same dish.

sections.title: Events, Tasks and Groups
sections.content:
A JSCalendar object is a JSON object that MUST be valid I-JSON, and property names and values are case sensitive. Every object names its type in @type. There are three top-level types, each with its own media type:

  • Event: a scheduled amount of time, such as a meeting, appointment, reminder or anniversary. It must start at a certain time and usually has a non-zero duration.
  • Task: an action item or to-do. It may start, be due, take an estimated time and recur, none of which is required.
  • Group: a collection of Event and/or Task objects, typically grouped by topic or calendar membership.

The RFC deliberately does not define a general normalization or equivalence method, because the right notion of equal (byte-level or semantic) depends on the use case. That is left to implementations and to the protocol that carries the data.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of things you can write down: an event, a to-do, and a folder that holds several of them.

sections.title: Data Types, Times and Patches
sections.content:
Beyond plain JSON types, the RFC defines a few precise ones. An Id is a string of 1 to 255 octets using only the base64url characters (letters, digits, hyphen, underscore). Maps keyed by Id are used in many places to represent unordered sets of objects that can be addressed by name. Int and UnsignedInt are limited to the safe range of a double-precision float, up to 2^53-1.

Times. A UTCDateTime is an RFC 3339 date-time with uppercase letters and the offset Z, and fractional seconds only when non-zero, so each moment has a single representation. A LocalDateTime has no offset. Its zone comes from the object's timeZone; with no zone it is floating, occurring at the same wall-clock time in whatever zone the user is in. When a local time falls in a DST discontinuity, the offset before the transition MUST be used. For example, 2020-11-01T01:30:00 in America/Los_Angeles becomes 2020-11-01T08:30:00Z.

Durations use a subset of ISO 8601 such as PT1H. Weeks and days are abstract and need not equal exact multiples of 24 hours, and leap seconds MUST NOT be considered.

PatchObject. A set of patches whose keys are JSON Pointer paths. A patch value of null removes a property, and any other value sets it. Patches cannot reach inside arrays, and one path cannot be the prefix of another. An implementation MUST reject the entire PatchObject if any patch is invalid, and MUST NOT apply partial patches.

Patches keep recurring-event exceptions small. Changing the location of the base event still flows into an occurrence that only patches something else.
sections.eli5: Times and lengths are written in strict, fixed formats so nobody can misread them. A patch is a sticky note that says only what changed.

sections.title: The Common Properties
sections.content:
Section 4 defines properties shared by the object types, in groups:

  • Metadata: uid (globally unique; UUID version 4 is RECOMMENDED), updated, created, prodId, relatedTo, and sequence, which starts at zero and MUST be incremented on every change except one that only modifies participants.
  • What and where: title, description, showWithoutTime for all-day events, locations, virtualLocations (with a mandatory uri), links, locale, keywords, categories and color.
  • Sharing and scheduling: priority (0 to 9, where 1 is highest), freeBusyStatus, privacy (public, private or secret), replyTo and participants.
  • Alerts: each Alert has a trigger, either an offset from the start or end or an absolute UTC time, and an action of display or email.
  • Multilingual and time zones: localizations map a language tag to patches that may only end in title, description or name. Custom zones in timeZones have identifiers that MUST start with / to avoid clashing with IANA names.

Each Participant must have at least one role (owner, attendee, optional, informational, chair or contact), and its participationStatus defaults to needs-action.

Type-specific properties come next. An Event has a mandatory start, a duration defaulting to PT0S, and a status defaulting to confirmed. A Task may have due, start, estimatedDuration, percentComplete and progress. A Group has mandatory entries and an optional source.
sections.eli5: Every event has a name tag, a place, a time, a guest list, and optional reminders. The rules say how to write each one down.

sections.title: Recurring Events
sections.content:
A recurring object has a base object with rules, not a copy per occurrence. The full recurrence set is built in order from recurrenceRules (generates date-times), excludedRecurrenceRules (removes date-times) and recurrenceOverrides (adds or excludes individual date-times and carries per-instance changes).

A RecurrenceRule maps the iCalendar RECUR type and has the same semantics. Its frequency is one of yearly, monthly, weekly, daily, hourly, minutely or secondly. It can also carry an interval (default 1), byDay, byMonthDay, byMonth, bySetPosition and others, and the range is limited by either count or until, never both. The rscale property selects a calendar system and defaults to gregorian, and skip (omit, backward or forward) says what to do with invalid dates.

The RFC spells out the expansion algorithm step by step, including rules that implicitly add bySecond, byMinute, byHour and similar parts taken from the initial date-time. The initial date-time is always the first occurrence, even if it does not match the rule.

In recurrenceOverrides, a key that matches no generated date-time is treated as an extra occurrence, like an iCalendar RDATE. A patch with excluded set to true removes that occurrence, like an EXDATE, and MUST NOT patch anything else. By default an occurrence inherits everything from the base object except its start, which shifts to the recurrence id.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing a weekly class on every Wednesday of the year, you write it once with a repeat rule, and then add notes like skip this Wednesday.

sections.title: Extensions and IANA Registries
sections.content:
Vendors MAY add custom properties, but the names MUST be prefixed by a domain name they control followed by a colon, for example example.com:customprop. The same prefixing applies to vendor-specific values and new object types. Vendors are strongly encouraged to register useful extensions rather than keep them vendor-specific.

IANA registered the media type application/jscalendar+json, which has a required type parameter with the values event, task or group. It also created three registries: "JSCalendar Properties", "JSCalendar Types" and "JSCalendar Enum Values". The properties registry follows the Expert Review process, and registrations cannot be deleted; a property that should no longer be used is declared obsolete.
sections.eli5: If you invent your own extra field, you put your website name in front of it so it never clashes with anyone else's.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC stresses that calendar data is very privacy sensitive: it can reveal a user's social network, locations and patterns of behavior. Because this document only defines the data format, protecting transmission and storage is mainly the concern of the API or storage method. Systems with real-world effects must authenticate the data they receive.

Specific risks it names:

  • Expanding recurrences: a rule may produce infinite occurrences or none at all, so implementations MUST avoid resource exhaustion and infinite loops when expanding or searching.
  • Time zones: events recur in the event's own zone, so a daylight saving change there can shift an occurrence for a user elsewhere, which could be used to make someone miss a meeting.
  • JSON parsing: the considerations of RFC 8259 apply, including care with unterminated structures and escape sequences.
  • URI values: fetching remote resources reveals IP information, and implementations should limit automatic fetching to avoid amplification attacks.
  • Spam and duplication: untrusted files can inject bogus events, and changing a UID on update can cause duplicate events.
sections.eli5: A calendar tells a lot about your life, so it must be kept safe. Programs also need care with tricky repeat rules that never end, and with calendar spam.

viz.caption: HOW THE RECURRENCE SET IS BUILT

items.title: 1. recurrenceRules
items.text: Generate the date-times on which the object occurs.

items.title: 2. excludedRecurrenceRules
items.text: Remove date-times from the generated set.

items.title: 3. recurrenceOverrides
items.text: Add extra date-times, exclude some, and patch individual instances.
